headline: South Korea's education minister quits over exam rules

chunks.text: On November 22, 2026, South Korea's education minister {{stepped down}}. He [[took responsibility]] for the [[confusion]] around the November 19 college entrance exam. Its scores help decide which universities students can attend. About half a million people {{signed up}} for it. In the days {{leading up to}} the exam, his ministry changed its rules against cheating many times. The president accepted his [[resignation]] within an hour.

chunks.text: The rules changed after a [[scandal]]. On November 15, the top scorer on a national exam for [[tax accountants]] [[admitted]] he had cheated with a tiny camera and AI. Two days before the college exam, the ministry {{brought in}} about 8,400 [[extra]] exam workers. Students had to cover their buttons with stickers, since a button can hide a camera. The ministry refused to {{put off}} the exam, saying a [[delay]] would cause more confusion. The ministry later said 111 [[test takers]] were caught with banned [[smart devices]].

chunks.text: On exam day, the government used its [[emergency alert]] system, which usually warns about disasters. Three times, a loud alarm {{went off}} on nearly every phone in the country, even silent ones. The goal was to {{pick out}} test takers who had kept phones against the rules. Two people from Japan [[translated]] the message to {{figure out}} why their phones rang. One person thought a war had {{broken out}}.

mainIdea.s: South Korea's education minister quit after his ministry made many quick changes to stop cheating on a huge exam. Students faced new rules, and alarms rang on phones across the country.
mainIdea.why: The minister stepped down over the confusion. In the days leading up to the exam, the rules changed many times, and alerts went off on nearly every phone.

mainIdea.s: The education minister left his job because officials found that many students used AI to get top scores on the college entrance test. Police are now checking every one of those results.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the AI scandal was on a different exam for tax accountants. The minister stepped down over the confusion caused by last-minute rule changes.

mainIdea.s: South Korea plans to move its college entrance test online next year to save money. Students will take it at home on their own computers, and teachers will check the answers by video.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a minister who stepped down. His ministry changed its rules against cheating many times before the exam.

lines.text: Did you hear that South Korea's education minister {{stepped down}}?
I did. Was it because of the AI cheating?
Sort of. It was more about the confusion before the college entrance exam. The rules kept changing [[on short notice]].
Two days before the test, they {{brought in}} about 8,400 extra workers. Students also had to cover every button with a sticker.
Stickers on buttons? That sounds like [[overkill]].
Maybe, but a button can hide a tiny camera. They checked everyone's glasses too.
That must have been so [[nerve-wracking]] for the students.
And then an alarm {{went off}} on almost every phone in the country, three times.
Wait, even on phones set to silent?
Yes. That would [[give me a heart attack]]. Someone even thought a war had {{broken out}}.
Kind of. It helped officials {{pick out}} some test takers with hidden phones. The ministry says 111 test takers were caught with banned smart devices.
Why didn't they just {{put off}} the exam?
The ministry said a delay would only make the confusion worse.
So a lot of people think the ministry [[dropped the ball]]?
A lot of lawmakers said so. The president accepted his resignation within an hour, and he'll choose someone to {{take over}}.
I still can't {{figure out}} why they changed so much so late.
